text:
On Tuesday afternoon Dwayne Wilson, 69, a thin Black man dressed in a light gray prison uniform, testified about the stifling heat he experienced in the Dade correctional institute, a concrete state prison south of Miami, Florida, without air conditioning. He removed his glasses and wiped his eyes as he spoke. “It was so hot,” he said, his voice catching. “It’s so hot sometimes you have to put water on the floor just to try to keep cool.”
Wilson said he’s housed in the H dorms, a T-shaped building with one-to-two-person cells, nicknamed “hell dorm” by prisoners because its concrete walls radiate heat absorbed from the sun. The plaintiff’s law firm, the Florida Justice Institute, convinced a judge to allow 31 sensors to be temporarily installed throughout the prison during the summer of 2025. They recorded temperature and humidity levels that Stefano Shiavon, a professor of civil and environmental engineering with expertise in thermal comfort, used to calculate the heat index. He found it to be above 88F (31C) 97% of the time, with the highest heat indexes often recorded at night, including one reading in the H dorm dayroom equivalent to 119F (48C) at 10pm one July day last year. “The walls sweat,” Wilson said. “It’s miserable in the cell at night because, again, it’s so hot. No air comes to the bed we sleep at and the bed is soaked in sweat.”
Wilson is among a group of prisoners who filed a lawsuit against the Florida department of corrections in 2024 for the conditions at the Dade correctional institution, alleging that the extreme heat contributed to four deaths and has subjected prisoners to cruel and unusual punishment. The bench trial began on Monday at a federal courthouse in downtown Miami serving the US district court for the southern district of Florida. The case comes amid growing concern over extreme heat in US prisons, where more than 40 states lack statewide policies requiring prisons to provide air conditioning, even as the climate crisis drives up summer temperatures and increases the risks.
Gary Wheeler, 67, who was also housed in the H dorms at the Dade correctional institute, testified that just months ago he thought he was having a heart attack, but upon going to the medical clinic in the prison he was told by a nurse that he had heat exhaustion. “I am worried about dying. I feel like sometimes when I go to sleep at night I’m not going to wake up in the morning,” he said. “My biggest fear is if I have a heatstroke and I can’t take care of myself, I have to depend on predators who could prey on you because you’re disabled.”
Both Wheeler and Wilson submitted informal grievances to the prison about the heat in the H dorms, some dating back to at least 2019. The men talked about another inmate affected by the heat named James “Jim” Beam, who was 83 years old, wheelchair bound, and had a respiratory condition. “He would breathe like he was gasping for air,” Wheeler said. “Every time he’d breathe he would throw his head back.”
Wilson said one night he woke up when he heard Beam hollering for help from his cell across the hall from him. “It was like 2am to 3am in the morning. He was on the floor,” Wilson said. Wilson helped Beam back into his wheelchair and brought him to the medical clinic, where he was put on a breathing treatment. But a doctor ended Beam’s treatment after about 30 minutes, after which Wilson pushed him back to his cell, he said. “The vent wasn’t working in the dorm. Jim’s tongue was kind of hanging out of his mouth and he was having problems breathing,” Wilson said. Within days, Beam died.
A medical examiner’s report found Beam’s death was caused by pneumonia, but Dr Susi Vassallo, an emergency medicine physician and medical toxicologist who has served as an expert witness in several cases involving heat in US prisons, testified that she believed long-term exposure to extreme heat contributed to his death, as well as the deaths of three other prisoners at the Dade correctional institute. Vassallo said that in no other case that she has participated in has there been such extensive heat data inside the prison. “It’s rather shocking, honestly,” she said of the temperatures and humidity levels captured by the sensors in the summer of 2025. “These are dangerous heat indices, putting these individuals at substantial risk of serious harm.”
In September, a US district court judge ruled that Texas must install air conditioning in all state prisons by the end of 2029. In that case, Vassallo had testified that air conditioning was the only way to reduce the heat and related risks of illnesses and deaths.
As rain pummeled the Miami courthouse on Wednesday, Vassallo said age, certain medical conditions and specific medicines can increase the risk of heat illnesses.
During their cross-examination of expert witnesses, attorneys for the Dade correctional institute argued that more than 100 ceiling and exhaust fans throughout the facility helped mitigate heat in the prison and that the eighth amendment prohibiting “cruel and unusual punishments” was not relevant. “In 1791, when the eighth amendment was ratified, there was no air conditioning,” said Mathew Gutierrez, defense counsel for the Florida department of corrections, FDC secretary Ricky Dixon and Dade correctional institution warden Francisco Acosta, in his opening statement on Monday. “So the lack of air conditioning could not have been encompassed in the eighth amendment.” Attorneys for the defendants also said that prisoners were permitted to wear shorts and had access to water jugs with ice during the summers. But prisoners said ice in the orange water coolers quickly melted because they were filled with hot water from the showers. Vassallo said that when temperatures reach a certain point, fans aren’t helpful, and they can actually increase body temperature.
Wilson has burn scars on much of his body from an incident in an Indiana jail when another inmate poured chemicals on the person in the bunk above his. On the areas of his body with chemical burns, he is unable to sweat. Wilson said he often gets itchy heat rashes when it’s hot in the prison. “When I move around, I can get scabbed up,” he said. “Then, with the rash that is on my body, it’s like it’s irritating to the point where it’s like burning.”
The trial is expected to resume next Monday, when more prisoners will testify about their experiences with heat at the Dade correctional institution, which can hold up to 1,500 people. Later, the prison and the Florida department of corrections will present their case.
digest_he:
אסירים במוסד הכליאה דייד שבפלורידה העידו במסגרת תביעה משפטית על חום קיצוני השורר במתקן נטול מיזוג האוויר, אשר לטענתם מגיע לדרגות מסוכנות הגורמות להם לסכנת חיים ממשית. חיישנים זמניים שהותקנו במקום הראו מדדי חום גבוהים במיוחד, לרבות בלילות, והתובעים טוענים כי התנאים הללו תורמים למקרי מוות ולפגיעות קשות בקרב האוכלוסייה הכלואה.

המדינה ורשויות הכליאה מצידן טוענות כי קיימים מאווררים רבים במתקן וכי האסירים זוכים למים מוצגים ואפשרות ללבוש בגדים קלים, וכי התיקון השמיני לחוקה אינו מחייב מיזוג אוויר מאחר ולא היה קיים בעת כתיבתו. המשפט מתנהל על רקע דאגה גוברת בארצות הברית ממקרי חום קיצוני בבתי סוהר והעדר מדיניות ארצית בנושא.
